figures.name: Léon Tolstoï
figures.presentation: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian novelist turned moral-religious critic, excommunicated by the Orthodox Church in 1901, addressed peasants and educated classes alike from his estate. His wave was the railway and the telegraph binding Imperial Russia — a society nine-tenths peasant — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was skeptical on two joined grounds: class — the telegraph served the “so-called cultured class” while the peasant heard “only the buzzing of the wires” — and moral-religious, judging technology by conscience and the Gospel; his instrument was voluntary moral renunciation, not law or force. No caricature: at 67 he learned to ride a bicycle with childlike pleasure. What instructs is the discipline of his recurring test — who benefits, who bears the cost, and by what standard a society should judge what it is told to call progress.
figures.epoch: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was a Russian novelist and moral-religious thinker whose later work turned from fiction toward social and ethical criticism. Alongside the fiction for which he was internationally known, he produced a substantial body of essays and treatises — "Progress and the Definition of Education" (1862), the autobiographical "A Confession" (written 1879–1882), the treatise "What Shall We Do?" (1886), "The Kingdom of God Is Within You" (1894), and "The Slavery of Our Times" (1900) — that made him a leading voice of Christian anarchism and pacifism. Writing from his estate in Imperial Russia, he addressed peasants and educated classes alike, and his moral authority extended well beyond literature. In 1901 the Russian Orthodox Church excommunicated him, a measure of how far his religious dissent unsettled the established institutions of his time.

figures.name: John Perry Barlow
figures.presentation: John Perry Barlow (1947–2018), Grateful Dead lyricist, Wyoming rancher and co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (1990), became a recognised voice of early cyberspace through The Economy of Ideas (1994) and A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace (1996). His wave was the internet’s leap from research networks to mass medium, met through The WELL and the legal frictions of a networking public — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. The record shows an unqualified enthusiast: cyberspace an emancipatory civilisation of the mind, beyond state sovereignty, ordered by ethics rather than imposed law — matched by years of unpaid civil-liberties advocacy. What instructs is this documented experiment in maximal techno-optimism: a utopian partly right about freedom, partly wrong about sovereignty, faithful to his thesis to the end.
figures.epoch: John Perry Barlow (1947-2018) was an American lyricist for the Grateful Dead, a Wyoming cattle rancher, and an internet-civil-liberties advocate whose life spanned strikingly different worlds. An early member of the pioneering online community The WELL, he co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation in 1990 with Mitch Kapor and John Gilmore, an organisation dedicated to defending civil liberties on networked systems, and he served on its board until his death; in 2012 he also co-founded the Freedom of the Press Foundation. His standing in the emerging digital culture rested less on technical work than on words: two texts made him a recognised voice of early cyberspace thought, A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace (Davos, 1996) and the essay The Economy of Ideas (Wired, 1994). He occupied an unusual position between counterculture, ranching and the networked frontier, which lent his advocacy its distinctive rhetorical register.

figures.name: Alan Turing
figures.presentation: Alan Turing (1912–1954), English mathematician, stood where mathematics, the first stored-program computers and the public debate over thinking machines met — a limit case in this study, since his wave is the direct ancestor of today's AI. His stance was confident advocacy with a method: replace the ill-defined “can machines think?” with a measurable test, predict openly, and demand “fair play for the machine.” He named the danger plainly — machines might “take control” — yet remained an advocate rather than a brake. What instructs is the lucidity: forecast, criterion and acknowledged risk held together in one stance.
figures.epoch: Alan Mathison Turing (1912–1954) was an English mathematician who worked at the centre of Britain's postwar computing effort. His documented career unfolded inside the state scientific establishment: wartime service at Bletchley Park, the National Physical Laboratory, and the University of Manchester. He addressed the London Mathematical Society on the prospects of automatic computing machines in February 1947, published "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" in the philosophy journal Mind in 1950, and wrote the first programming manual for the Manchester Electronic Computer (Mark II) in 1951. He also circulated the National Physical Laboratory report "Intelligent Machinery" (1948) and took part in BBC radio discussions of machine thinking in 1951 and 1952. He thus stood at the meeting point of mathematics, the emerging discipline of computing, and the public debate over whether machines could think.

title.en: Enforceable audits, not voluntary pledges
title.fr: Des audits contraignants, pas des promesses volontaires

text.en: In January 2026 testimony on New York's AI Act, Chowdhury argues that AI governance belongs in 'enforceable obligations, not voluntary ethics pledges.' The most meaningful safety improvements, she testifies, come when evaluations are run by bodies structurally independent of product and revenue teams — so companies' and their experts' in-house safety assurances should not be taken on trust but checked by mandatory independent audit. She personifies 'trust, but independently verify.'
text.fr: Dans son témoignage de janvier 2026 sur la loi new-yorkaise sur l'IA, Rumman Chowdhury soutient que la gouvernance de l'IA relève d'« obligations contraignantes, et non de promesses éthiques volontaires ». Les améliorations les plus significatives, témoigne-t-elle, viennent d'évaluations menées par des entités structurellement indépendantes des équipes produit et commerciales — les garanties internes des entreprises et de leurs experts ne doivent donc pas être crues sur parole, mais vérifiées par des audits indépendants obligatoires. Elle incarne le « faire confiance, mais vérifier de façon indépendante ».

arguments.reference: Testimony of Dr. Rumman Chowdhury before the New York State Senate Standing Committee on Internet and Technology, on the New York Artificial Intelligence Act, 15 January 2026.
arguments.quote: The most meaningful improvements have come when evaluations are run by entities structurally independent of product and revenue teams and when results are tied to concrete risk-mitigation obligations.

title.en: The Dutch childcare benefits scandal (toeslagenaffaire)
title.fr: Le scandale néerlandais des allocations familiales (toeslagenaffaire)

text.en: The Dutch tax administration used automated risk profiling, including a risk-scoring algorithm, to flag suspected childcare-benefit fraud; roughly 26,000 parents were wrongly treated as fraudsters, with discriminatory effects linked to nationality and dual citizenship. The parliamentary inquiry report 'Ongekend onrecht' ('Unprecedented Injustice', 17 December 2020) found fundamental institutional failures, and the entire Rutte III government resigned on 15 January 2021. The case is widely cited to show that public institutions themselves can deploy and defend harmful algorithmic systems for years.
text.fr: L'administration fiscale néerlandaise a utilisé un profilage automatisé des risques, dont un algorithme de scoring, pour repérer des fraudes présumées aux allocations de garde d'enfants ; environ 26 000 parents ont été traités à tort comme fraudeurs, avec des effets discriminatoires liés à la nationalité et à la double nationalité. Le rapport d'enquête parlementaire « Ongekend onrecht » (« Une injustice sans précédent », 17 décembre 2020) a constaté des défaillances institutionnelles fondamentales, et l'ensemble du gouvernement Rutte III a démissionné le 15 janvier 2021. Ce cas est largement cité pour montrer que les institutions publiques elles-mêmes peuvent déployer et défendre pendant des années des systèmes algorithmiques préjudiciables.

title.en: Andrew Ng: extinction fears serve incumbents' regulatory agenda

arguments.person: Andrew Ng, co-founder of Google Brain, professor at Stanford University

text.en: In October 2023, Andrew Ng — co-founder of Google Brain and professor at Stanford — argued in an interview with the Australian Financial Review that some large technology companies amplify fears of AI-driven human extinction in order to obtain regulation that would weaken open-source competition. His warning is a contemporary version of the regulatory-capture argument: rules presented as protecting the public may in fact be shaped to serve incumbent interests.

Son avertissement est une version contemporaine de l'argument de la capture réglementaire : des règles présentées comme protégeant le public peuvent en réalité être façonnées pour servir les intérêts des acteurs établis.

figures.name: Norman Borlaug
figures.presentation: Norman Borlaug (1914–2009), American agronomist and 1970 Nobel Peace laureate, directed the wheat-breeding work in Mexico that grew into the Green Revolution. His wave was agriculture’s synthetic-chemistry transformation — chemical fertilizer he called the fuel of its forward thrust, synthetic pesticides, improved seed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was the enthusiast’s: deploy fast, at scale, to feed the poorest, defending transgenic crops and condemning “antiscience zealotry.” Yet the optimism was conditional and moral, not naïve: the Nobel lecture calls the Green Revolution a temporary success, a breathing space, grounded in food as a moral right. What instructs is urgency to deploy joined to an explicit statement of the technology’s limits and ethical purpose.
figures.epoch: Norman Ernest Borlaug (1914–2009) was an American agronomist and plant pathologist who directed the cooperative wheat-improvement work that developed high-yielding, disease-resistant dwarf wheat varieties, first in Mexico within the Rockefeller Foundation programme that later grew into the CIMMYT research centre. Trained in the North American land-grant scientific tradition, he became one of the most publicly recognised agricultural scientists of the mid-twentieth century, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for the yield gains his methods brought to wheat and rice cultivation in the developing world. His standing rested not on a single theoretical work but on a body of field-based breeding practice and on widely circulated statements of its purpose — chief among them the 1970 Nobel lecture, "The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity," which framed the enterprise as a moral response to hunger.

figures.name: Paul Berg
figures.presentation: Paul Berg (1926–2023), American biochemist and 1980 Nobel laureate in Chemistry, built the first recombinant DNA molecules — the opening act of genetic engineering, a technology whose promise and hazards were debated before either was fully known. Facing that uncertainty he chose a rare course: in 1974 he led the call for a voluntary moratorium on the riskiest experiments, then chaired the 1975 Asilomar Conference that resumed them under graded containment rules of the community's own making — while later resisting over-restrictive legislation. His trajectory — pause, then proceed under the field's own rules — remains the textbook case of a science governing itself before being governed, wary equally of unmanaged risk and of heavy outside control.
figures.epoch: Paul Berg (1926-2023) was an American biochemist and one of the leading molecular biologists of the postwar United States. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 for his fundamental studies of nucleic acids, and his Nobel Lecture, "Dissections and Reconstructions of Genes and Chromosomes" (Stockholm, 8 December 1980), documents the work for which he is best known: the construction of the first recombinant DNA molecules, joining genetic material from different organisms and reshaping the working methods of molecular biology (berg1980-nobel). Beyond the bench, he occupied a position of scientific authority in his community, chairing the National Academy of Sciences committee that examined the hazards of the new techniques and convening, as its chairman, the 1975 Asilomar Conference that set the terms under which the field would proceed (berg1974-letter, berg1975-asilomar).

figures.name: Yoshua Bengio
figures.presentation: Yoshua Bengio (born 1964), co-founder of modern deep learning, 2018 Turing Award laureate, recorded as the field’s most-cited researcher, lived the very wave this study takes as its subject: artificial intelligence itself, whose acceleration past GPT-4-class systems he judged to have outrun precaution and governance. From inside, he revised his position on public evidence — first scientific signatory of the 2023 pause letter, Senate testimony for regulation “beyond voluntary guidelines,” chair of the 2025 International AI Safety Report — while continuing to build: the deliberately non-agentic “Scientist AI” and the nonprofit LawZero (2025). A living figure still in motion, he models how precaution and retained optimism can coexist without collapsing into boosterism or doom.

title.en: The EU AI Act's conformity assessment regime
title.fr: Le régime d'évaluation de la conformité de la législation européenne sur l'IA

text.en: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) requires high-risk AI systems to undergo a conformity assessment before being placed on the EU market (Article 43). For certain categories — notably biometric systems — assessment by an independent notified body is required when harmonised standards are not (fully) applied, and compliant systems carry the CE marking familiar from European product-safety law. The regime institutionalises the idea that official certification can give users a reasoned basis for confidence they could not obtain by individual inspection.
text.fr: Le règlement (UE) 2024/1689 (législation sur l'IA) impose aux systèmes d'IA à haut risque une évaluation de la conformité avant leur mise sur le marché européen (article 43). Pour certaines catégories — notamment les systèmes biométriques — l'évaluation par un organisme notifié indépendant est requise lorsque les normes harmonisées ne sont pas (pleinement) appliquées, et les systèmes conformes portent le marquage CE bien connu du droit européen de la sécurité des produits. Ce régime institutionnalise l'idée qu'une certification officielle peut donner aux utilisateurs une base raisonnée de confiance qu'ils ne pourraient obtenir par un examen individuel.

title.en: Aviation safety: expert judgement vindicated at scale
title.fr: La sécurité aérienne : le jugement des experts validé à grande échelle

text.en: Commercial aviation is the standard example of a domain where deferring to expert safety judgement has demonstrably worked. According to IATA's 2024 Safety Report (released 26 February 2025), the all-accident rate was 1.13 per million flights — one accident per 880,000 flights across 40.6 million flights — and the five-year average improved from one accident per 456,000 flights (2011–2015) to one per 810,000 (2020–2024). This record was built on expert-run certification, audits and independent accident investigation, a model often invoked for AI assurance.
text.fr: L'aviation commerciale est l'exemple type d'un domaine où la déférence au jugement des experts en sécurité a manifestement fonctionné. Selon le rapport de sécurité 2024 de l'IATA (publié le 26 février 2025), le taux global d'accidents était de 1,13 par million de vols — un accident pour 880 000 vols sur 40,6 millions de vols — et la moyenne quinquennale s'est améliorée d'un accident pour 456 000 vols (2011–2015) à un pour 810 000 (2020–2024). Ce bilan repose sur la certification par des experts, les audits et l'enquête indépendante sur les accidents, un modèle souvent invoqué pour l'assurance de l'IA.

figures.name: Erwin Chargaff
figures.presentation: Erwin Chargaff (1905–2002), Austrian-born biochemist who established the base-composition rules of DNA, became in later life a humanistic critic estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had made possible. His wave was genetic engineering — recombinant DNA creating new forms of life from the early 1970s — this study’s mirror for today’s AI, promoted largely by its own developers. His stance was deep skepticism: a new form of life, once released, cannot be recalled; no one holds the right to counteract “irreversibly, the evolutionary wisdom of millions of years”; and scientists’ self-regulation cannot weigh a risk borne by all humanity. What instructs is the method more than the verdict — irreversibility first, and those who profit are not the only ones entitled to judge safety. Documentary richness, never a moral model.
figures.epoch: Erwin Chargaff (1905-2002), an Austrian-born biochemist who made his scientific career in the United States, established the base-composition regularities known as Chargaff's rules — that in DNA adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine — findings his own work, drawing on chromatographic methods, made central to the study of nucleic acids. An eminent figure of mid-twentieth-century biochemistry and author of Essays on Nucleic Acids (Elsevier, 1963), he became in later life a humanistic critic and memoirist. His Heraclitean Fire: Sketches from a Life before Nature (The Rockefeller University Press, 1978) presents him as a scientist steeped in classical learning who grew estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had helped make possible. He remained within the scientific establishment while increasingly standing apart from it.

figures.name: Ōe Kenzaburō
figures.presentation: Ōe Kenzaburō (1935–2023), Japanese novelist and 1994 Nobel laureate in Literature, formed by the humanism of his teacher Kazuo Watanabe, became a public conscience on the atomic question with Hiroshima Notes (1965). His wave was atomic energy and weapons, met at the point of consequence, not invention — Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the 1954 Bikini test, then Fukushima in 2011 — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was victim-side across five decades: reading the atom “through the eyes of the victims of nuclear power,” and after Fukushima fusing weapons and civil nuclear power into a single refusal, carried into the ten-million-signature Sayonara Genpatsu campaign. What instructs is the method rather than the verdict: those who bear a technology’s consequences, not only its advocates, must be heard before it is scaled.
figures.epoch: Ōe Kenzaburō (1935–2023) was a Japanese novelist and essayist awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1994; his Nobel lecture, "Japan, the Ambiguous, and Myself," delivered 7 December 1994, deliberately set his work against Kawabata's earlier "Japan, the Beautiful, and Myself." Formed by the humanism of his teacher Kazuo Watanabe, a scholar of Rabelais, he built a body of fiction and reportage centred on human vulnerability and moral witness. His documentary work Hiroshima Notes, serialized in the journal Sekai in 1964–65, published by Iwanami Shoten in 1965 and read for this study in its English translation, established him as a public conscience on the atomic question. The birth of his son Hikari, who lived with a disability and found healing through music, recurs across his writing as a source of what he called "the exquisite healing power of art." He remained an engaged public intellectual until his death in 2023.

figures.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
figures.presentation: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), British naturalist and co-discoverer of evolution by natural selection, largely self-taught, was also a social reformer and, by the 1890s, a prominent public figure of British science. His wave was the germ theory and the medical revolution it enabled — above all smallpox vaccination, reaching ordinary life as state power through Britain’s compulsory Vaccination Acts — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. Toward vaccination he was a documented skeptic: treating it as “a purely statistical question,” he examined the mortality figures himself and condemned the practice and its penal enforcement, insisting official assurances “must never be accepted without verification.” The posture is double-edged, and that is what instructs: his statistical case was found erroneous by the Royal Commission and later epidemiology, vaccination among scientific medicine’s great successes — a reminder that data-literate, principled dissent can still reach the wrong conclusion.
figures.epoch: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) was a British naturalist who, independently of Charles Darwin, arrived at the principle of natural selection, making him a co-discoverer of evolution by natural selection. Largely self-taught across surveying, natural history and statistics, he spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay Archipelago before returning to a public career in British science. His authority extended well beyond biology: in The Wonderful Century (1898) he surveyed and celebrated his era's scientific triumphs, and his autobiography My Life (1905) records a restless intellect drawn to heterodox causes. He was also a committed social reformer, serving as the first president of the Land Nationalisation Society (1881) and arguing, in Land Nationalisation (1882), that land was a common inheritance. By the 1890s he was a prominent public figure in British science.

title.en: IEA: AI's own energy appetite versus the climate

text.en: The International Energy Agency's April 2025 report "Energy and AI" projects that global data-centre electricity demand will roughly double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 — slightly more than Japan's entire electricity consumption today. This complicates the claim that AI will help solve climate change: the tool meant to help fight emissions is itself a fast-growing source of electricity demand. In the debate, this is the authoritative counterpoint — AI may aid some grand challenges while worsening the resource footprint of others.

Cela complique l'idée que l'IA aidera à résoudre le changement climatique : l'outil censé aider à combattre les émissions est lui-même une source à croissance rapide de demande électrique. Dans le débat, c'est le contrepoint faisant autorité — l'IA peut aider certains grands défis tout en aggravant l'empreinte d'autres.

title.en: 1954: nuclear electricity "too cheap to meter"

arguments.person: Lewis L. Strauss, Chairman of the US Atomic Energy Commission

text.en: In September 1954, Lewis Strauss, chairman of the US Atomic Energy Commission, told science writers that the atomic age would shortly deliver electricity too cheap to meter, famines known only as history, and much longer lifespans. Seventy years later, none of these everyday-life promises materialised on anything like that horizon. The historical pattern — revolutionary technologies systematically overpromising on the ten-to-twenty-year everyday horizon — is the strongest documented reason for discounting similar promises made today for AI.
text.fr: En septembre 1954, Lewis Strauss, président de la Commission américaine à l'énergie atomique, annonçait aux journalistes scientifiques que l'ère atomique apporterait bientôt une électricité trop bon marché pour être facturée, des famines reléguées aux livres d'histoire et des vies bien plus longues. Soixante-dix ans plus tard, aucune de ces promesses de vie quotidienne ne s'est réalisée à un tel horizon. Ce schéma historique — les technologies révolutionnaires surpromettent systématiquement à l'horizon de dix à vingt ans — est la raison documentée la plus forte pour relativiser les promesses analogues faites aujourd'hui pour l'IA.

figures.presentation: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti (1876–1944), Italian poet and impresario of the avant-garde, founded Futurism with the 1909 manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro. His wave was the motor-aviation complex — racing car, aeroplane, the whole machine age of speed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was unqualified exaltation, the wave’s machine-worship extreme: “a roaring motor car… is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace,” “Time and Space died yesterday,” danger and rupture embraced as first principles. He instructs as a limit case: a genuine aesthetic response to a new technology hardening into a doctrine that scorns caution, restraint and every voice of the past. His standing in the pre-war avant-garde rested less on a single masterwork than on his role as impresario and theorist of a self-declared break with the museums, academies and inherited culture of his day.

figures.name: Nikola Tesla

title.en: The EU AI Act: harm is being pre-empted by law

arguments.person: European Parliament and Council of the European Union

text.en: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689), in force since August 2024, is the world's first comprehensive AI law. It grades systems from minimal to unacceptable risk, outright bans practices such as social scoring, and imposes strict duties on high-risk uses, with penalties up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of global turnover. Its existence is the counter-argument to the lasting-damage thesis: harmful uses are precisely those society is now legally structured to prevent, so durable damage is a policy failure to be avoided, not a foregone conclusion.
text.fr: Le règlement européen sur l'intelligence artificielle (Règlement 2024/1689), en vigueur depuis août 2024, est la première loi complète sur l'IA au monde. Il classe les systèmes du risque minimal au risque inacceptable, interdit purement des pratiques comme la notation sociale, et impose des obligations strictes aux usages à haut risque, avec des amendes allant jusqu'à 35 millions d'euros ou 7 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial. Son existence est le contre-argument à la thèse du dommage durable : les usages nuisibles sont précisément ceux que la société est désormais légalement organisée pour prévenir, si bien que le dommage durable est un échec de politique publique à éviter, non une fatalité.

figures.presentation: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975), German-born political theorist exiled to the United States, analysed how modern societies think, judge and act in common, from The Human Condition (1958) to “Lying in Politics” (1971). title.en: Rio Principle 15: the precautionary approach

text.en: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, adopted by the UN Conference on Environment and Development, codifies the precautionary approach: 'Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation.' Transposed to AI, it grounds the position that when potential harms are serious or irreversible, one does not wait for real-world trial results before acting — study and prevention come first.

figures.name: Bertolt Brecht
figures.presentation: Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956), German playwright and theorist of epic theatre, treated the stage as an instrument of critical reason “in the scientific age.” His wave was mass media — Weimar radio and cinema, cultural production in the hands of broadcasters and film capital — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. He was a conditional, reformist enthusiast: radio was “one-sided when it should be two” and had to pass “from distribution to communication,” letting the listener speak as well as hear — but only once its ownership was transformed, since “only the State can organize this.” What instructs: he locates a technology’s value not in the apparatus but in who owns and organises it. That enthusiasm was inseparable from his committed Marxism, a position of the figure to weigh rather than adopt.
figures.epoch: Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was a German playwright, poet, and theatre theorist whose work reshaped the dramaturgy of the Weimar Republic and the decades that followed. Formed in the theatrical and literary milieu of 1920s Germany, he became the theorist of what he called epic theatre, codified in his mature essay "A Short Organum for the Theatre" (written 1948, published 1949), in which he defined the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) meant to keep "the spectator's intellect free and highly mobile." His output included The Threepenny Opera, over whose film adaptation he later litigated, and he worked as writer and collaborator across theatre, radio, and cinema. Committed to a Marxist reading of art and society, Brecht treated the playhouse as an instrument for critical reason "in the scientific age" rather than for emotional catharsis.

figures.name: Thomas Edison
figures.presentation: Thomas Edison (1847–1931), American inventor who made invention itself an organised industrial enterprise, built the phonograph and a standardised central-station lighting system. His wave was electricity — lamps, motors and generating stations moving from laboratory demonstration to contested public utility — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was pragmatic enthusiasm: an invention was worth what it did and what it sold, machinery “the greatest of emancipators,” tempered by method — one per cent inspiration, several thousand things that won’t work. Disclosure is owed: in the war of currents his camp ran a denigration campaign against alternating current, including public electrocutions of animals, his own 1889 article serving that commercial interest. He instructs by holding enthusiasm, empirical discipline and self-interest together — documentary richness, not a moral model.
figures.epoch: Thomas Alva Edison (1847-1931) was an American inventor and inventor-entrepreneur who made invention itself into an organised industrial enterprise. He worked at the centre of the United States' electrical and machine age and, by the late 1870s, had introduced the phonograph, which he set out and championed in his own article 'The Phonograph and Its Future' in The North American Review (1878), written months after building the device. He went on to develop an electric-lighting system organised around standardised central-station generation, alongside motors and machinery. His authorized biography (Dyer and Martin, 1910) and later collections such as The Diary and Sundry Observations (posthumous, 1948) record a figure whose standing rested less on theory than on a prolific record of working, marketable inventions.

figures.name: Galilée
figures.presentation: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian mathematician and natural philosopher, heard a rumour of a Dutch spyglass, rebuilt a better instrument within weeks, turned it on the sky — and went from observation to published book in about eight weeks. He then spent decades defending “sense experiences and necessary demonstrations” against consecrated authority, mocking the philosophers who refused to look through the telescope. His posture is early, active adoption: trust instrument-aided evidence over inherited authority, and iterate in the open. The record also keeps its costs — a thirteen-year self-embargo out of fear of ridicule, the frank pursuit of patronage, and the coerced abjuration of 1633, evidence of the control regime he lived under.
figures.epoch: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian mathematician and natural philosopher of the late Renaissance. By his own account in Il Saggiatore (1623), he was reappointed and confirmed for life in his professorship of mathematics at the University of Padua at double his previous salary, and he subsequently entered the service of the Medici court of Tuscany. His principal works span a compressed public career: the observational booklet Sidereus Nuncius (1610), the doctrinal Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), the polemical Il Saggiatore (1623), and the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632). His earlier correspondence with Johannes Kepler (1597, 1610) documents that his Copernican convictions predate his fame and place him in exchange with a leading astronomer of the age. He worked within a world whose epistemic authority rested with the university Aristotelians and the doctrinal organs of Counter-Reformation Rome.

text.en: Ng gives the most cited technical objection to the statement: 'prove it's safe' is proving a negative, and no engineer can guarantee a general technology will never be misused. figures.name: Neil Postman
figures.presentation: Neil Postman (1931–2003), American educator and cultural critic, built across Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985) and Technopoly (1992) a sustained critique of a culture reorganising itself around the screen. His wave was the personal computer and the networked information machine, promoted as a cure for information scarcity — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was cultural-critical skepticism, not luddism: “every technology is both a burden and a blessing,” each innovation “a Faustian bargain” carrying an embedded epistemological, political or social prejudice — proceed “with our eyes wide open so that we may use technology rather than be used by it.” He supplied the practical instrument — what is the problem to which this technology is the solution, and whose problem is it? — and lived the posture, writing longhand, owning no computer. What instructs is the discipline: name the trade-offs, ask who benefits, require a tool to justify itself before adoption.

figures.name: Tim Berners-Lee
figures.presentation: Tim Berners-Lee (b. 1955), English computer scientist, invented the World Wide Web at CERN (1989–1991) and made the decision that shaped it: releasing its standards royalty-free, open for anyone to build on. The wave he set in motion turned a network of machines into a universal information space — then drifted, as he documented himself, toward data silos and a few dominant platforms. His answer is the disillusioned optimist's: naming the Web's dysfunctions in his anniversary letters, then building remedies — Solid, Inrupt, the Contract for the Web — to re-decentralise personal data. He models optimism as conditional and revisable: a hope held open to evidence, paired with the labour of repair.
figures.epoch: Tim Berners-Lee (b. 1955, England) is an English computer scientist who, while working at CERN between 1989 and 1991, designed and built the first Web browser and server together with the HTTP and HTML specifications that define the World Wide Web. In 1994 he founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the standards body he continued to shape for decades, and in 1999 he set out the project's founding vision in the memoir Weaving the Web. The 2017 ACM A.M. Turing Award citation recognised the fundamental protocols and algorithms allowing the Web to scale. Across five decades he remained an active builder rather than a retired founder, launching the Solid project and the company Inrupt in 2018. His standing rests less on a single discovery than on a sustained decision, documented in his own account, to release the Web's standards royalty-free — kept open for anyone to implement without patent or fee.

figures.name: Norbert Wiener
figures.presentation: Norbert Wiener (1894–1964), American mathematician and founder of cybernetics, specified early computer design and helped build cybernetic prostheses — the technology arrived through his own hands. His wave was the high-speed computing machine and the automation it made possible, his “second industrial revolution,” spreading into factory, governance and warfare — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was cautionary rather than pessimistic: automation a “two-edged sword,” a learning machine able to outrun its designer, and once an irreversible process is launched “we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire.” He set moral “know-what” above technical “know-how,” and in 1947 refused to supply guided-missile research he judged dangerous. What instructs is technical fluency paired with restraint: those best placed to build a powerful technology may owe the clearest account of what it should not be trusted to decide.

His principal works span the technical (Cybernetics, 1948) and the popular-philosophical (The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950; God & Golem, Inc., 1964, awarded the 1965 National Book Award posthumously). By mid-century he was both an originator of the new science and a widely read public interpreter of it.

figures.name: Louis Pasteur
figures.presentation: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), French chemist, was not a commentator on his era's disruptive wave but its principal architect: germ theory, and the medicine it made possible. His optimism was total — the new science as “a law of peace, of work, of salvation” — but never naive: enthusiasm, he insisted, must keep “a severe control as its inseparable companion.” His method was proof-first and public: at Pouilly-le-Fort he signed the protocol in advance and let a controlled trial decide before witnesses; at the human frontier he treated the child Joseph Meister “not without grave and cruel misgivings.” What instructs is the pairing: confident enthusiasm disciplined by demonstrated proof and restraint.
figures.epoch: Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) was a French chemist whose work reached from crystallography and fermentation into medicine. His Sorbonne conference of 7 April 1864 argued against spontaneous generation; his 1881 report to the Academie des sciences recorded the public anthrax-vaccine trial at Pouilly-le-Fort; and in November 1888 the Institut Pasteur was inaugurated in Paris before President Sadi Carnot. He held standing across the era's academies of sciences, of medicine, and the Academie francaise, both as an experimenter and as a public figure.

figures.presentation: George Orwell (1903–1950), English essayist and novelist, watched the mass-media wave — radio and cinema reaching millions at once — from the inside as a BBC producer, and against it as its most lucid critic. His posture is accept-but-distrust: the machine had to be accepted “as one accepts a drug — grudgingly and suspiciously”; he used radio to bring poetry to a wide audience while scrutinising who controlled it, and later dramatised its surveillance potential in Nineteen Eighty-Four. figures.name: Karl Marx
figures.presentation: Karl Marx (1818–1883), German political economist and revolutionary organiser, analysed industrialisation not as an inventor but as a scholar — reading the factory inspectors' reports in London to trace how steam-driven machinery restructured labour. His stance is dialectical: the same machine is emancipatory in itself, gifted with “the wonderful power of shortening and fructifying human labour,” yet degrading in the hands of capital, where it lengthened the working day. He rejected the Luddite response — target the mode in which machines are used, never the instruments themselves — and backed factory legislation as society's conscious reaction. His enduring lesson: separate a technology's potential from the social arrangements that govern its deployment.

With Friedrich Engels he issued the Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848); his principal work, Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Volume I, appeared in 1867. He also drafted the founding texts of the International Working Men's Association -- its Inaugural Address (1864) and the Instructions for the delegates of the Geneva Congress (1866) -- writing these in English. His method rested on close reading of official statistics, parliamentary Blue Books, and the reports of the English factory inspectorate, which he re-argued through his own analysis. By the 1860s he stood among the more systematic critical theorists of industrial society, though his wider influence grew mostly after his death.

figures.name: Audrey Tang
figures.presentation: Audrey Tang (born 1981), Taiwanese programmer risen from the free-software world to become Taiwan’s first Digital Minister (2016–2024) and first openly non-binary cabinet member, distilled the island’s digital-democracy practice into Plurality (2024). Her wave is artificial intelligence itself, met from an unusual vantage — the engineer who builds the systems and the official who governs their public use, deploying AI-assisted “broad listening” for national-scale consultation while confronting deepfakes and algorithmic amplification. Her stance is democratic optimism conditional on democratic design: AI governance “must be a race to safety, not a race to power,” each community able to set its own norms, harms like “addictive intelligence” read as design choices that can be made otherwise. A living figure still in motion, she shows how a builder can advocate diffusion and precaution at once — catastrophe neither inevitable nor negligible, but contingent on institutions.
figures.epoch: Audrey Tang (born 1981 in Taipei) is a Taiwanese programmer and public servant who rose from the free-software world into government. A self-taught coder, she became a Silicon Valley software founder at nineteen and led the Pugs open-source project before entering Taiwan's civic-technology movement. In 2016 she was appointed Taiwan's first Digital Minister, a post she held until 2024, and she was the island's first openly non-binary cabinet member. Her fullest intellectual statement is the open-source book Plurality: The Future of Collaborative Technology and Democracy (2024), co-authored with the economist E. Glen Weyl and a wider contributor community, which distils Taiwan's digital-democracy practice — vTaiwan, the Polis opinion-clustering tool, the g0v civic-hacker movement — into a general design programme. She is best understood as a practitioner-theorist of participatory governance rather than an academic.

figures.name: José Martí
figures.presentation: José Martí (1853–1895), Cuban poet and journalist exiled in New York from 1880, chronicled the Gilded-Age metropolis for Latin American readers until his death in the Cuban war of independence he had helped organise. His wave was electricity and its engineering — Edison’s light, the telegraph, the Brooklyn Bridge he chronicled in 1883 — watched from inside the technological metropolis, yet as a Latin American outsider. His stance was genuinely double: delight at the new force — Edison a “Dantesque figure,” the Bridge “a ponderous arm of the human mind,” electricity soon to relieve suffering labour — while the same texts warn of a prosperity “empty of spirit” and insist his republics graft the world onto their own trunk rather than be absorbed. What instructs is the discipline: he knew that world “from inside” (viví en el monstruo), quantified it honestly, and refused both uncritical adoption and reflexive rejection.
figures.epoch: José Martí (1853-1895) was a Cuban poet, essayist and journalist. From 1880 he lived as an exile in New York, where he wrote the Escenas norteamericanas — chronicles for Latin American periodicals such as La Nación (Buenos Aires), La América and La Revista Ilustrada (New York), and La Pluma (Bogotá). His principal texts of this period include the prologue to Pérez Bonalde's Poema del Niágara (1882), "Coney Island" (1881), "El puente de Brooklyn" (1883), the essay "Nuestra América" (1891) and "La verdad sobre los Estados Unidos" (1894); his last, unfinished letter to Manuel Mercado was written at Dos Ríos on 18 May 1895, the eve of his death in the Cuban war of independence he had helped organise. He remains a national figure of Cuba.

figures.name: Wangari Maathai
figures.presentation: Wangari Maathai (1940–2011), Kenyan biologist — the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate — founded the Green Belt Movement and received the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize. Her wave, read through her own testimony, was industrial, commercialised, top-down development: forests cleared for commercial plantations, household food crops displaced, public land grabbed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. Her stance was precautionary, aimed at destructive, imposed development rather than technology as such: “there can be no development without sustainable management of the environment,” justice and ecological integrity worth more “than profits at any cost,” and agency located in the community — “solutions to most of our problems must come from us.” What instructs is less opposition to a technology than the insistence that its deployment be equitable, sustainable and locally governed; her Nobel lecture closed on conditional hope: “The choice is ours.”
figures.epoch: Wangari Maathai (1940-2011) was a Kenyan biologist and environmental campaigner. Trained as a research scientist, she was, per the dossier, the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, later serving as a professor of veterinary anatomy. She founded the Green Belt Movement, a grassroots tree-planting and citizen-education initiative. As that year's laureate, she delivered the Nobel Peace Prize Lecture in Oslo on 10 December 2004. Her principal written works, the memoir Unbowed (2006), The Challenge for Africa (2009), and Replenishing the Earth (2010), set out her account of the movement, her critique of top-down development, and her spiritual environmentalism. She combined scientific credentials with sustained public activism, standing against the Kenyan state in campaigns such as the Uhuru Park (1989) and Karura Forest (1998-99) disputes.

arguments.person: Friedrich A. Hayek, economist, Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences 1974

text.en: In his classic 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', economist and later Nobel laureate Friedrich Hayek argued that the knowledge relevant to economic and social decisions never exists in one place, but is scattered among countless individuals. This argument is regularly invoked against uniform top-down rule-making for fast-moving technologies: an international rule-setter would lack the local, contextual knowledge that dispersed decision-makers hold.
text.fr: Dans son essai classique de 1945, « The Use of Knowledge in Society », l'économiste et futur lauréat du prix Nobel Friedrich Hayek soutenait que le savoir pertinent pour les décisions économiques et sociales n'existe jamais en un seul lieu, mais est dispersé entre d'innombrables individus. Cet argument est régulièrement invoqué contre l'édiction de règles uniformes venues d'en haut pour des technologies en évolution rapide : un régulateur international manquerait du savoir local et contextuel détenu par des décideurs dispersés.

arguments.reference: American Economic Review, vol. 35, no. 4, September 1945, pp. 519–530 (full text verified at Econlib)
arguments.quote: The peculiar character of the problem of a rational economic order is determined precisely by the fact that the knowledge of the circumstances of which we must make use never exists in concentrated or integrated form but solely as the dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals possess.

figures.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
figures.presentation: Robert Oppenheimer (1904–1967), American theoretical physicist, directed the Los Alamos laboratory where the first atomic weapons were built, then moved into postwar science policy — the Acheson-Lilienthal report, the AEC’s General Advisory Committee. His wave was the atom, reaching the world through his own hands and entering public consciousness with Hiroshima and Nagasaki — this study’s mirror for today’s AI as a dual-use capability contested first by its own makers. His stance was genuinely ambivalent: the work an “organic necessity,” yet within weeks of Hiroshima the warning that mankind would come to curse the names of Los Alamos and Hiroshima; in 1948, that the physicists had “known sin”; in 1949, the recommendation against the hydrogen Super, and candour and international control against secrecy. What instructs is measured, not heroic: a maker holding capability and restraint together, judging a technology while implicated in it.
figures.epoch: Julius Robert Oppenheimer (1904-1967) was an American theoretical physicist who became, during the Second World War, the scientific director of the Los Alamos laboratory, the centre where the first atomic weapons were designed and built. His standing rested less on a single discovery than on his ability to lead a large scientific community at the frontier of physics, and afterwards to speak for it in public life. From this base he moved into the institutions of postwar science policy: he was the principal scientific author of the 1946 Acheson-Lilienthal report on international control of atomic energy, and he chaired the General Advisory Committee of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. In 1953 he delivered the BBC Reith Lectures, published as Science and the Common Understanding. He was thus at once an insider who built the technology and a widely heard interpreter of what it meant.

figures.name: Ibn Khaldun
figures.wave: Crafts and techniques of urban civilisation
figures.presentation: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406), Arab scholar, jurist and chief judge in Cairo, founded in the Muqaddima (1377) a new science of civilization explaining why societies rise, flourish and decay. The disruptive capability of his world was the crafts of settled urban life — building, writing, calculation, medicine — which he showed arise with the city and multiply where societies are large, stable and strongly governed. His stance is analytic rather than advocative: technique is a distinctively human power whose crafts “give intelligence” to their practitioners, yet whose perfection is tied to the life-cycle of civilization — they recede as the city declines. Neither boosterism nor alarm: a causal account of technology as inseparable from the social order that sustains it.
figures.epoch: Abd ar-Rahman Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) was an Arab scholar, jurist and administrator born in Tunis, active across the Maghrib and later in Mamluk Egypt, where he served as a Maliki chief judge in Cairo. His standing rests on the Muqaddima (1377), the introductory volume of his universal history Kitab al-'Ibar, in which he set out to found a new science of human social organization ('umran) explaining why civilizations rise, flourish and decay. The publisher's description of Rosenthal's translation credits the work with having established the foundations of several fields, including the philosophy of history, sociology, ethnography and economics (Rosenthal 1958). Rather than a chronicler of dynasties, he presented himself as an analyst of their underlying causes, cross-checking transmitted reports against what a settled society could plausibly support.

figures.name: Érasme
figures.presentation: Erasmus (1466–1536), among the foremost humanists of the northern Renaissance, edited the first published Greek New Testament (1516) and lived inside Europe’s leading presses — Aldus in Venice, Froben in Basel — arguably the first author to build a career entirely on print. His wave was the printing press, multiplying texts at unprecedented speed and filling the world, as he complained, with “swarms of new books” of every quality — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. He was a critical adopter: among the technology’s heaviest professional users and one of its sharpest critics — printers “so grasping and mercenary” that errors stand — calling for public remedy: magistrates against abuse, law against fraud, subsidy for works of common use. One asymmetry is disclosed: he used the press fully for himself while at times seeking to limit others’ use of it.
figures.epoch: Desiderius Erasmus (1466-1536), born in the Netherlands, ranks among the foremost humanist scholars of the northern Renaissance. He built his career on classical and biblical philology, producing the Adagia (a continually expanded compendium of proverbs, from 1500), the Colloquies, and, in 1516, the Novum Instrumentum omne — the first published Greek New Testament, edited from the manuscript evidence rather than accepted on the authority of the received Vulgate (Froben, Basel). He worked inside the leading presses of Europe, living in Aldus Manutius's Venetian shop in 1508 and in Johann Froben's Basel household across 1514-1516 and again 1521-1529. His writings circulated on an unusual scale for the period — roughly 1,260 printings and reprintings before his death, on one scholarly estimate — making him arguably the first European author to build an entire career on the medium of print.

title.en: The Bletchley Declaration: AI risks framed as 'inherently international'

text.en: At the first AI Safety Summit (Bletchley Park, 1–2 November 2023), governments including the United States, China and the European Union signed a joint declaration stating that 'many risks arising from AI are inherently international in nature, and so are best addressed through international cooperation'. figures.name: Walter Benjamin
figures.presentation: Walter Benjamin (1892–1940), German critic and philosopher of media, wrote from exile after the Nazi seizure of power and died in 1940 fleeing the regime; he was also a working broadcaster, with some eighty Weimar radio programmes. His wave was mass media — cinema and radio, mechanical reproduction dissolving the “aura” of the unique artwork while film capital and the fascist state bent the same apparatus toward the star cult and the aestheticisation of politics. His stance was dialectical: promise and peril held in one view, the remedy never to ban but to turn consumers into producers. His Marxism and sympathy for the Soviet reorganisation of the media are positions of the figure, disclosed as such — selection for documentary richness, never moral endorsement. What instructs is the discipline of seeing both at once.
figures.epoch: Walter Benjamin (1892–1940) was a German literary critic, essayist, and philosopher whose work ranged across aesthetics, media, and cultural history. Its landmarks include the aphoristic One-Way Street (Einbahnstraße, 1928), the Little History of Photography (1931), the essay The Storyteller (1936), and his best-known text, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, first published in French in the Institute for Social Research's Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung in 1936. Unusually for a theorist, he was also a working broadcaster, writing and presenting some eighty radio programmes between 1927 and 1933. He wrote from exile after the Nazi seizure of power, and died in 1940 in flight from the regime. His standing today rests less on any academic post than on the enduring influence of these essays on media and cultural theory.

figures.name: Fei-Fei Li
figures.presentation: Fei-Fei Li (born 1976), Stanford computer scientist, initiated ImageNet in 2009 and co-founded the Institute for Human-Centered AI; her wave is artificial intelligence itself, the deep-learning turn her own benchmark helped catalyse — a direct contemporary witness rather than a historical mirror. Her stance is human-centered and deliberately two-sided: machines as partners “enhancing us, not replacing us”; government urged to lead ethical deployment; caution against extinction hype in favour of near-term bias and misinformation; “govern on the basis of science, not science fiction.” She nonetheless opposed California’s SB 1047 as mis-aimed. A living figure still in motion, she models holding optimism and guardrails together, calibrating rules to demonstrated, application-specific risk.
figures.epoch: Fei-Fei Li (b. 1976), whose path from a childhood in China to education and a career in the United States is recounted in her memoir The Worlds I See, is a computer scientist whose career has centred on Stanford University, where she is a professor and, since 2019, co-founder and co-director of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI), an institute whose mission is to "advance AI research, education, policy, and practice to improve the human condition." In 2009 she initiated ImageNet, the large-scale labelled image dataset that became a canonical benchmark of the field. She served as chief scientist for AI/ML at Google Cloud (2017-2018), co-founded the non-profit AI4ALL (2017), and in 2024 founded the startup World Labs. That 2023 memoir, together with frequent public testimony, has made her a widely cited voice — popularly styled the "Godmother of AI", the label Bloomberg's 2024 profile carries in its very title — at the intersection of machine-learning research and technology policy.

figures.name: Shen Kuo
figures.presentation: Shen Kuo (1031–1095), scholar-official of Song China — astronomer, finance commissioner, diplomat, military commander — retired to his Dream Brook estate and wrote the Mengxi Bitan, six hundred jottings on techniques and natural phenomena. There he preserved the only record of movable type and of Bi Sheng, the uncredentialed artisan who invented it: without Shen's notebook, both would be unknown. His verdict is sober and quantified — of little use for two or three copies, “marvellously quick” for hundreds or thousands. His method instructs more than his verdict: learn how a technology actually works, judge it by demonstrated results rather than by the authority of its makers, and preserve the name of the person who built it.
figures.epoch: Shen Kuo (1031–1095) was a scholar-official of Northern Song China whose career ran through the empire's technical and administrative institutions. Sivin's Dictionary of Scientific Biography records his appointment to direct the Bureau of Astronomy (1072), his service on the Finance Commission, his appointment as a Hanlin academician (1076), a diplomatic embassy to the Liao (1075) and a military command at Yanzhou (1080–81). After a fall from favour in 1082 he retired to his Dream Brook (Mengxi) estate, where he completed his best-known work, the Mengxi Bitan (Brush Talks from Dream Brook, also rendered Dream Pool Essays), around 1088 — a notebook of some six hundred jottings recording and evaluating techniques, natural phenomena and administrative affairs. In modern scholarship he stands as an observer of unusual range across the practical knowledge of Song China.

figures.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
figures.presentation: Joseph Weizenbaum (1923–2008), German-born American computer scientist who fled Nazi Germany, built ELIZA at MIT in 1966 and became a critic of artificial intelligence from within the field. His wave was mid-century computing recast as candidate reasoning — judgment, diagnosis, even psychotherapy proposed for delegation — met as a builder: ELIZA showed him how readily people attribute understanding to software. His stance was skeptical in a specific register, moral-categorical rather than technical: “there are certain tasks which computers ought not be made to do, independent of whether computers can be made to do them” — deciding distinguished from choosing, calculation from judgment — while never rejecting computing itself, arguing for the rational use of science and technology. What instructs is balanced, technically literate criticism: caution from one who had mastered the tools, distinguishing what a technology can do from what it should be asked to do.
figures.epoch: Joseph Weizenbaum (1923–2008) was a German-born American computer scientist who became a prominent critic of his own field from within it. Having fled Nazi Germany in the mid-1930s, he worked from 1955 on a General Electric team that built the first computerized banking system for the Bank of America, then joined MIT in 1963, where he became professor of computer science. He authored the SLIP programming language and, in 1966, the ELIZA program — a natural-language conversation simulator published in Communications of the ACM that became one of the era's most widely discussed artifacts. His 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation established his international reputation as a critic of artificial intelligence from within the field. He remained engaged in public debate until his death in Berlin in 2008.

figures.name: Léon Tolstoï
figures.presentation: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian novelist turned moral-religious critic, excommunicated by the Orthodox Church in 1901, addressed peasants and educated classes alike from his estate. His wave was the railway and the telegraph binding Imperial Russia — a society nine-tenths peasant — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was skeptical on two joined grounds: class — the telegraph served the “so-called cultured class” while the peasant heard “only the buzzing of the wires” — and moral-religious, judging technology by conscience and the Gospel; his instrument was voluntary moral renunciation, not law or force. No caricature: at 67 he learned to ride a bicycle with childlike pleasure. What instructs is the discipline of his recurring test — who benefits, who bears the cost, and by what standard a society should judge what it is told to call progress.
figures.epoch: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was a Russian novelist and moral-religious thinker whose later work turned from fiction toward social and ethical criticism. Alongside the fiction for which he was internationally known, he produced a substantial body of essays and treatises — "Progress and the Definition of Education" (1862), the autobiographical "A Confession" (written 1879–1882), the treatise "What Shall We Do?" Writing from his estate in Imperial Russia, he addressed peasants and educated classes alike, and his moral authority extended well beyond literature. figures.name: Henry Adams
figures.presentation: Henry Adams (1838–1918), American historian and man of letters, cast his Education as a study in whether a nineteenth-century mind could meet the forces of the coming century. His wave was electricity — the dynamo above all, met in the great hall of the 1900 Paris Exposition, coal-output doubling every ten years by his reckoning — this study’s mirror for today’s AI: an irruption of forces “totally new.” His stance was the anxious skeptic’s: awe and dread before a power outrunning human moral and mental capacity — “science will be the master of man,” he wrote as early as 1862 — yet not apocalyptic, the outcome a “toss-up between anarchy and order.” What instructs is that measured anxiety: a cultured observer registering, early, that a technology may accelerate faster than institutions and minds can absorb. In candour, his private correspondence contains documented antisemitic passages — documentary richness, not a moral model.
figures.epoch: Henry Adams (1838-1918) was an American historian and man of letters whose principal work, the autobiographical The Education of Henry Adams, was privately printed in 1907 and first published for the wider public in 1918. Writing of himself in the third person, he cast his life as a study in whether nineteenth-century education could equip a mind for the forces of the coming century. His documented reflections on technological acceleration recur across four decades: an 1862 letter to his brother Charles Francis Adams Jr., written from London during the American Civil War, already voiced the anxiety he later theorised in the essay "The Rule of Phase Applied to History" (written 1909). He stood not as a policy-maker or engineer but as a cultured observer, and his writing left a lasting mark on American letters.

figures.name: Jean Trithème (Johannes Trithemius)
figures.presentation: Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), German Benedictine abbot of Sponheim and figure of monastic humanism, grew his abbey’s library from some forty-eight to two thousand volumes and wrote what is widely described as the first printed book on cryptography. His wave was the printing press, developed near his world at Mainz, met at close range in the transition from scriptorium to press. His stance, in De Laude Scriptorum (1492), was measured skepticism, not rejection: parchment outlasts paper — “the printed book is a thing of paper and in a short time will decay entirely” — and hand-copying is a formative spiritual discipline. Yet the documented paradox: he had that very treatise printed, and filled his library with printed books. What instructs is the separation of reasoned caution from reflexive refusal — naming specific concerns while adopting the new medium where it served his ends: principled reservation and practical use need not exclude each other.
figures.epoch: Johannes Trithemius (Jean Trithème, 1462-1516) was a German Benedictine abbot and a notable figure of monastic humanism in the German Renaissance. Abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, he pursued a reforming programme centred on learning: he expanded the abbey's library from roughly forty-eight to some two thousand volumes, printed books included. A prolific author across several fields, he remains best known for the treatise De Laude Scriptorum (In Praise of Scribes), composed in 1492. He also produced the cryptographic writings Polygraphia (composed 1508, printed 1518), widely described as the first printed book on cryptography, and Steganographia (composed around 1499), alongside the historical chronicle Annales Hirsaugienses. Noël L. Brann's intellectual biography presents him as a central representative of the reforming, book-centred monastic culture of his time.

figures.name: Erwin Chargaff
figures.presentation: Erwin Chargaff (1905–2002), Austrian-born biochemist who established the base-composition rules of DNA, became in later life a humanistic critic estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had made possible. His wave was genetic engineering — recombinant DNA creating new forms of life from the early 1970s — this study’s mirror for today’s AI, promoted largely by its own developers. His stance was deep skepticism: a new form of life, once released, cannot be recalled; no one holds the right to counteract “irreversibly, the evolutionary wisdom of millions of years”; and scientists’ self-regulation cannot weigh a risk borne by all humanity. What instructs is the method more than the verdict — irreversibility first, and those who profit are not the only ones entitled to judge safety. Documentary richness, never a moral model.
figures.epoch: Erwin Chargaff (1905-2002), an Austrian-born biochemist who made his scientific career in the United States, established the base-composition regularities known as Chargaff's rules — that in DNA adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine — findings his own work, drawing on chromatographic methods, made central to the study of nucleic acids. An eminent figure of mid-twentieth-century biochemistry and author of Essays on Nucleic Acids (Elsevier, 1963), he became in later life a humanistic critic and memoirist. His Heraclitean Fire: Sketches from a Life before Nature (The Rockefeller University Press, 1978) presents him as a scientist steeped in classical learning who grew estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had helped make possible. He remained within the scientific establishment while increasingly standing apart from it.

text.en: Michael Sandel argues that engineering human traits reflects a drive to master what should be received as a gift, eroding humility and solidarity. On the 'disagree' side it provides a philosophically serious objection to enhancement that is not merely fear of risk. The moderator can use it to raise what is lost, not just what is gained.
text.fr: Michael Sandel soutient que façonner les traits humains traduit une volonté de maîtriser ce qui devrait être reçu comme un don, érodant l'humilité et la solidarité. Du côté « désaccord », il fournit une objection philosophiquement sérieuse à l'augmentation, qui n'est pas une simple peur du risque. Le modérateur peut soulever ce qui se perd, et pas seulement ce qui se gagne.

arguments.reference: 'The Case Against Perfection', The Atlantic, April 2004
arguments.quote: The problem with eugenics and genetic engineering is that they represent the one-sided triumph of willfulness over giftedness, of dominion over reverence, of molding over beholding.

text.en: I am in favour of technologies that raise human mental abilities beyond their natural level.
text.fr: Je suis favorable aux technologies qui portent les capacités mentales humaines au-delà de leur niveau naturel.

clarification.en: This statement is about technologies that push mental abilities — such as memory, attention, or reasoning — above what a person could reach naturally. It is about going beyond the natural level, not about treating illness or repairing a loss.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur des technologies qui poussent les capacités mentales — comme la mémoire, l'attention ou le raisonnement — au-dessus de ce qu'une personne pourrait atteindre naturellement. Il s'agit de dépasser le niveau naturel, pas de soigner une maladie ni de réparer une perte.

text.en: Humanity should use technology to overcome its biological limits.
text.fr: L'humanité devrait utiliser la technologie pour dépasser ses limites biologiques.

clarification.en: This statement is about humanity as a whole: should we use technology to go past the limits our bodies and minds are born with, such as ageing or the limits of strength and memory? It is about going beyond those natural limits, not about curing illness or injury; and it is about the general direction, not about any single device.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur l'humanité dans son ensemble : devrions-nous utiliser la technologie pour dépasser les limites avec lesquelles nos corps et nos esprits naissent, comme le vieillissement ou les limites de force et de mémoire ? Il s'agit de dépasser ces limites naturelles, pas de soigner les maladies ou les blessures ; et de la direction générale, pas d'un dispositif en particulier.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means you firmly believe humanity should not use technology to go beyond its biological limits; those limits should be accepted.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que vous pensez fermement que l'humanité ne devrait pas utiliser la technologie pour dépasser ses limites biologiques ; ces limites devraient être acceptées.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you firmly believe humanity should use technology to overcome its biological limits wherever it can.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous pensez fermement que l'humanité devrait utiliser la technologie pour dépasser ses limites biologiques partout où elle le peut.

examples.fr: Par exemple, la recherche pourrait viser à ralentir ou arrêter le vieillissement pour que les gens vivent beaucoup plus longtemps en bonne santé.

figures.name: Isocrate
figures.presentation: Isocrates (436–338 BCE), Athenian teacher of discourse, was led by a weak voice away from live oratory toward the written speech, his lifelong medium and the basis of his influential school. His wave was writing itself — prose composed, revised and circulated as fixed text where eloquence had lived in oral performance — this study’s mirror for today’s AI, and the medium his contemporary Plato distrusted. His stance was enthusiastic but disciplined: the power of speech is what let humans found cities, make laws and invent arts — “there is no institution devised by man which the power of speech has not helped us to establish” — yet competence demands aptitude, practice and a teacher’s exact instruction, and misuse is answered by education and public criticism, not prohibition. What instructs is the committed adopter who insisted the new medium serve the common good, governed by formation rather than unchecked release or ban.
figures.epoch: Isocrates (436–338 BCE) was an Athenian teacher and writer of prose discourse, active across the fourth century BCE. By his own account in the Panathenaicus (9–10), a weak voice and a temperament unsuited to public affairs led him away from live oratory and toward composing written speeches, which became his lifelong medium; he ran an influential school of discourse in Athens. His surviving works, consulted here in George Norlin's Loeb translation via the Perseus Digital Library, include Against the Sophists (c. 390), the Panegyricus (380), Nicocles, the Antidosis (c. 354), To Philip (346), and the Panathenaicus, completed in his nineties. In the Antidosis (7) he presents that written corpus as "a true image of my thought and of my whole life." He stands in this study as the enthusiast voice of the writing wave, the documented counter to Plato's suspicion of the written word.

figures.name: Ada Lovelace
figures.presentation: Ada Lovelace (1815–1852), English mathematician formally excluded from her era’s institutions — the Royal Society admitted no women — worked through private tutelage beside Babbage and De Morgan. Her wave was the birth of programmable computation, met as a working annotator: her 1843 translation of Menabrea’s memoir on the Analytical Engine, with signed Notes three times its length, among the first documents to treat the machine as a general symbol-manipulator that “might act upon other things besides number.” Her stance was enthusiasm disciplined by analysis: the engine “weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves,” yet “has no pretensions whatever to originate anything” — augmentation, not replacement, paired with verification, down to the grave error she caught in Babbage’s own computation. What instructs is the method: imagine a technology’s reach while calibrating its claims and checking them oneself.
figures.epoch: Augusta Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) was an English mathematician who worked at the edge of her era's mathematical science while formally excluded from its institutions: the Royal Society admitted no women, and her access was mediated through private tutelage and correspondence. From 1840 she studied under the mathematician Augustus De Morgan (Hollings, Martin and Rice, 2017), and moved in a circle that included Charles Babbage, De Morgan and Mary Somerville. Her published scientific output was concentrated in a single work: her 1843 English translation of L. F. Menabrea's memoir on Babbage's Analytical Engine, to which she appended her own signed Notes A-G (Taylor's Scientific Memoirs, vol. 3, pp. 666-731). By Babbage's later testimony the Notes ran to roughly three times the length of the memoir they annotated (Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, 1864).

figures.name: Galilée
figures.presentation: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian mathematician and natural philosopher, heard a rumour of a Dutch spyglass, rebuilt a better instrument within weeks, turned it on the sky — and went from observation to published book in about eight weeks. He then spent decades defending “sense experiences and necessary demonstrations” against consecrated authority, mocking the philosophers who refused to look through the telescope. His posture is early, active adoption: trust instrument-aided evidence over inherited authority, and iterate in the open. The record also keeps its costs — a thirteen-year self-embargo out of fear of ridicule, the frank pursuit of patronage, and the coerced abjuration of 1633, evidence of the control regime he lived under.
figures.epoch: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian mathematician and natural philosopher of the late Renaissance. By his own account in Il Saggiatore (1623), he was reappointed and confirmed for life in his professorship of mathematics at the University of Padua at double his previous salary, and he subsequently entered the service of the Medici court of Tuscany. His principal works span a compressed public career: the observational booklet Sidereus Nuncius (1610), the doctrinal Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), the polemical Il Saggiatore (1623), and the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632). His earlier correspondence with Johannes Kepler (1597, 1610) documents that his Copernican convictions predate his fame and place him in exchange with a leading astronomer of the age. He worked within a world whose epistemic authority rested with the university Aristotelians and the doctrinal organs of Counter-Reformation Rome.

title.en: Vita-More: the right to augment body and brain
title.fr: Vita-More : le droit d'augmenter le corps et le cerveau

text.en: Natasha Vita-More gives the agree side an articulate woman's voice grounded in decades of transhumanist thought. She frames enhancement not as vanity but as morphological freedom: your body and brain are yours to improve, and no one may forbid it. A respondent who values autonomy over their own mind will recognise her argument that choosing a memory implant is a right, not a transgression.
text.fr: Natasha Vita-More apporte au camp du « oui » une voix féminine articulée, ancrée dans des décennies de pensée transhumaniste. Elle présente l'augmentation non comme de la vanité mais comme une liberté morphologique : votre corps et votre cerveau vous appartiennent et nul ne peut vous en interdire l'amélioration. Un répondant attaché à l'autonomie sur son propre esprit reconnaîtra son argument selon lequel choisir un implant de mémoire est un droit, non une transgression.

arguments.reference: Natasha Vita-More, The Transhumanist Manifesto (original 1983; v.4, 2020).
arguments.quote: augmentation and enhancement to the human body and brain are essential

title.en: A scientific call to accept cognitive enhancement

text.en: In a 2008 Nature commentary, seven scientists and ethicists led by Henry Greely argued society should stop treating 'enhancement' as a dirty word and manage safe cognitive-enhancing drugs for healthy people. It documents a mainstream, peer-visible position favouring raising mental abilities. The moderator can present it as the scientific-community version of the 'agree' side.

Cela documente une position visible et sérieuse favorable à l'élévation des capacités mentales. Le modérateur peut la présenter comme la version scientifique du côté « accord ».
